item.title: Forget petrodollars, ‘chip-dollars’ show U.S. power now flows from tech dominance—but the new currency regime is ‘inherently riskier,’ analyst says
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of the shift in global economic power from petrodollars to chip-dollars, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Semiconductors are surpassing oil as the linchpin of the dollar’s global reach, demonstrating U.S. technological might but also revealing a less stable foundation, according to Deutsche Bank.

In a note last week, foreign exchange strategist Mallika Sachdeva pointed out that for the first time in modern history, global trade in chips now exceeds trade in oil and gas. Excluding China, Asia’s surplus in the chip trade matches petroleum-related surpluses in the Persian Gulf, she added.

That’s as AI hyperscalers keep ramping up capital expenditures, which are expected to top $1 trillion next year, further propping up chip trade flows.

“The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of U.S. power — from geopolitical to technological leadership,” Sachdeva wrote, adding that the so-called petrodollar is quickly being superseded by the new “chip-dollar.”

The petrodollar regime goes back to a deal struck in 1974 when Saudi Arabia agreed to price its oil in dollars and invest surpluses in U.S. assets, especially Treasury debt. In return, the American military ensured security in the region and free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And because oil is a core input to global manufacturing and transport, supply chains have a natural incentive to dollarize. Indeed, Mideast oil and gas are used to make petrochemicals, fertilizer, and even helium.

But the underpinnings of the petrodollar are breaking down due to the Iran war as Tehran exposes the limits of the U.S. military, while the AI boom is sending a tsunami of capital from Asia to the U.S.

This time around, rather than Mideast kingdoms recycling oil-trade surpluses into U.S. debt, Asia’s chip behemoths are recycling chip-trade surpluses into U.S. stocks. In fact, South Korean households have 90% of their equity exposure in the U.S., according to Deutsche Bank. Overall, foreign purchases of U.S. equities are now more than double that of Treasuries.

“The emerging chip-dollar regime is one where US technology leadership is motivating global savings to be reinvested in U.S. companies — providing funding for the US corporate sector to make enormous investments in new technology such as AI,” Sachdeva explained.

Chip dominance begets dollar dominance

Just like how oil penetrated industrial supply chain, chips are embedded in the digital economy as inputs in consumer electronics, automobiles, computers, communication devices, and AI systems. She estimated chips account for more than 50% of the capex for a data center.

And despite Asia’s dominance in chipmaking, 70% of the industry’s profits flow to U.S. firms. In addition, the key countries in the supply chain of advanced chips are friendly with Washington, namely Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

“The potent combination of U.S. control over key upstream technologies and intellectual property, alongside a supply chain located in U.S. allies has given the U.S. enormous control over chips,” Sachdeva added.

At the same time, chips ensure continued dollar dominance in global trade, payments, capital markets, and private sector savings, while also supporting America’s AI buildout, she pointed out.

But Deutsche Bank cautioned that the new currency regime has a “circularity” risk because capital flowing from Asian chip hotspots provides financing to U.S. companies driving the AI boom. That means if consumer demand for compute can’t support AI investments, earnings for tech companies would come down—as well as chip demand.

The focus on stocks over debt means more instability too. U.S. stocks overall are three times as volatile as Treasuries—and tech stocks are up to 10 times as much, Sachdeva noted.

“A dollar driven by chips, AI and private capital connections should be inherently riskier,” she warned.

That risk was on display in recent weeks as tech stocks sold off sharply on fears the AI boom was about to go bust. And although Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday sparked a big rebound, the Trump administration is cracking down on foreign access to U.S. AI technology, potentially curbing the chip trade.

Dollar vs. yuan — Coke vs. Pepsi

To be sure, threats to the dollar’s status as the global reserve currency have come and gone over the decades. More recently, the proliferation of U.S. financial sanctions has given countries more reason to diversify away from the dollar.

But no credible alternatives have emerged yet, despite China’s aggressive efforts to internationalize the yuan.

China facilitates its use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets. Beijing also promotes “China prices,” or yuan benchmarks on domestic commodity exchanges. Chinese banks have more than doubled their yuan lending to overseas borrowers since 2023, and the central bank has reached currency swap agreements with dozens of peers.

But Zongyuan Zoe Liu, senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relation, argued in Foreign Affairs last month that Beijing doesn’t actually want to replace the dollar on the world stage.

“Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy,” she wrote.

“From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.”

item.title: How Jensen Huang's return as NVIDIA's CEO is going over in China
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Explains the impact of Jensen Huang's return as CEO of NVIDIA on China's tech industry, with useful context for an English learner.

How Jensen Huang's return as NVIDIA's CEO is going over in China

In China, Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO is being met with a mixed reaction – as Beijing weighs whether it wants the US company's chips at all.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

Jensen Huang now has his job back at NVIDIA. Whether China should have access to NVIDIA's best computer chips - that debate is now back, too. And how is all this playing out in China? Well, we've reached NPR's Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Hi there.

JENNIFER PAK, BYLINE: Hi.

SUMMERS: Jennifer, you're there in Beijing. Tell us what you've been hearing from people.

PAK: Well, from the general public, some say this whole saga of Jensen Huang's swift fall and sudden return is kind of like a microdrama. I don't know if you're familiar with these. These are super popular, kind of like soap operas. They're broken down into bite-size episodes, two to three minutes each, super fast pace. And just like a microdrama, this Huang scandal has had a lot of twists and turns.

In China's tech circles, the views are split. I spoke to Du Chen, a technology media editor at Ifanr in Beijing. He says one group believes Huang's conduct raises serious ethical violations and shouldn't be in charge. While the other group, he says, are ones who have had business dealings with NVIDIA or interacted with Huang directly and indirectly.

DU CHEN: (Speaking Chinese).

PAK: This group, he says, generally trusts Huang's ability as the company's CEO and believes he would return, just not as fast as it happened, like 11 days.

SUMMERS: It was really fast, yeah. Now, what about the allegation that China launched a spy operation targeting NVIDIA and Huang? Has there been much discussion about that?

PAK: China's foreign ministry has denied these spy allegations. NPR has just heard that in the U.S., congressional staff have been briefed by American intelligence officials. And a person familiar with the matter said there is no evidence the woman who had an affair with NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang, named Alice Huang - of no relation - is a Chinese spy, though she is believed to have passed along information to the Chinese after the affair started.

Now, here in China, there's surprisingly little talk on the ground, not just because of censorship, says Du, the Chinese tech media editor we just heard from earlier. He says people here don't believe that Alice Huang was a spy. They were photographed openly. As for allegations that she and her company, Megaspeed, helped to smuggle NVIDIA chips to China, well, Du doesn't know the specific details, but he says...

DU: (Speaking Chinese).

PAK: While many people in the West, he says, may have heard about this for the first time through the U.S. media, you know, about NVIDIA chips entering China through gray channels, these are not a secret in China at all, he says, especially within the tech industry.

SUMMERS: Well, Jensen Huang has said that he wants to be able to sell chips directly to China. So I wonder, is there hope for smoother access to those high-end U.S. chips?

PAK: Maybe among some Chinese AI companies, but the expectation among industry watchers I've been speaking to say Washington is likely going to tighten export controls, and it already has. Now, in Beijing, there's been conflicting messages coming from officials because on the one hand, officials have been criticizing the U.S. for these export controls. At the same time, when the U.S. does approve chips for sale to China, Beijing has told its companies not to buy them, to buy local.

So to make sense of this, I asked Steven Hai, who is an assistant professor of technology entrepreneurship at the Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University. He says, think of China's central government not as a monolith.

STEVEN HAI: They want normal global trade, but they want so-called, like, its own developmental strategy in the long run.

PAK: So short- to medium-term, he says, China wants access to NVIDIA's high-end chips until it can build up its own replacement, something that Jensen Huang has wanted to avoid.

SUMMERS: NPR China correspondent Jennifer Pak in Beijing, thank you.

PAK: Thank you.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

item.title: The AI boom helped lift retirement accounts, but the Nvidia whiplash showed how much investors’ financial futures depend on a handful of stocks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discusses the influence of a few tech stocks on retirement accounts, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Millions of Americans, and their financial futures, may be exposed to the recent AI-fueled swings in the market regardless of whether they’ve ever used a chatbot.

Stocks plunged Wednesday morning before recovering much of the loss. Near the start of trading, the Dow fell more than 1,000 points and the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% as AI chip stocks sold off for a second straight day. Nvidia fell as much as 8%. By late afternoon, the S&P 500 had cut its loss to about half a percent, and the Dow had turned higher.

Wednesday’s swing capped a week in which a single company’s board decision moved the index that holds much of Americans’ retirement accounts. Roughly two-thirds of of Fidelity 401(k) savers keep everything in a target-date fund.

Following a tumultuous few weeks in which Jensen Huang resigned and was later reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker’s stock jumped 31%, added about $950 billion in market value, and lifted the S&P 500 by 4.7%. Still, the S&P 500 is now about 8% below its Oct. 6 record. Last Friday it closed 11.6% below that high, putting it in correction territory, after seven straight losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

Stock market concentration has been on the rise for years, and it is now near 35-year highs. Just 10 stocks in the S&P 500 account for about 39% of its total market capitalization, with the five largest stocks—all tech giants—alone accounting for 29%, according to Charles Schwab. That means an American with $100,000 in an index fund tied to the S&P 500 would have $29,000 in just five stocks.

As a result, many investors may think they are putting money into a diversified investment when the health of their portfolios may actually be tied more to the fate of a handful of tech giants than they realize, said Martin Mulyadi, a professor of accounting at Shenandoah University’s College of Business, Engineering & Technology.

“An index fund spreads your money across 500 companies, but it does not spread the risk evenly,” he told Fortune.

For the millions of Americans who have poured their money into S&P 500 index funds through their 401(k)s, this concentration has been a boon in recent years. A booming stock market that has risen just over 50% during the past five years helped push the number of 401(k) millionaires at Fidelity to a record 769,000 in June. Even before the selloff began, that number had fallen some 2% between the second and third quarters, but was still up 15% from a year earlier, according to Fidelity.

Through the third quarter, the vast majority of retirement savers were still investing. About 96% of 401(k) participants at Fidelity either maintained or increased their savings rate during the third quarter, the financial services company revealed in a report this week.

“Despite market volatility, many workers continue to increase their savings, stay invested, and take advantage of workplace retirement plan features designed to support long-term success,” Sharon Brovelli, Fidelity’s president of workplace investing, said in a statement.

Yet the growing dominance of a handful of technology giants means even those who have followed conventional retirement wisdom and have added to diversified funds may be exposed to heightened risk.

A further stock slide could hurt the portfolios of millions of Americans and especially for those closer to retirement: The average Fidelity 401(k) millionaire is 58 years old.

Retirement at risk

For older Americans, a downturn early in retirement could have implications for when they can afford to stop working and how much money they’ll have to live on once they do.

By selling investments at depressed prices to cover living expenses, retirees face the problem of sequence-of-returns risk. If a falling stock market in early retirement causes retirees to sell their investments at lower prices, that means they have less money left in the market that could later benefit from an eventual recovery.

To try to avoid this phenomenon, Charles Schwab recommends maintaining a short-term reserve of low-risk and more liquid investments that retirees could draw from in a downturn to avoid touching their portfolio.

The increasing concentration of the stock market also doesn’t necessarily mean investors should abandon index funds altogether. Investors should instead consider taking a closer look at the makeup of their portfolio, said Sean McEvilly, the managing partner and founder of Vistamark Investments.

“The practical move isn’t to bail out of stocks. It’s to look at the whole 401(k), since target-date and large-cap funds often hold the same names, and make sure there’s real exposure to small and midsized companies, international stocks, and bonds,” McEvilly told Fortune.

item.title: Credit card perks are fueling airline profitability
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analyzes the role of credit card perks in airline profitability, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Credit card perks are fueling airline profitability

So, airlines are pitching more and more specialty brand credit cards on your flight.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Thanksgiving brings some of the busiest days of the year for airlines. The industry is now paying high fuel prices, but airlines have a card up their sleeves, or really, their customers do. We are talking about loyalty credit cards. For airlines, those cards help balance their bottom line. NPR's Bill Chappell reports.

BILL CHAPPELL, BYLINE: American Airlines made a big splash with its frequent flyer loyalty program 45 years ago. Here's part of an ad from the 1980s.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR: We invented the advantage program for frequent fliers, so all those business miles can add up to free vacation trips. We even keep track of your miles for you automatically.

CHAPPELL: Within a few years, airlines were partnering with banks to issue branded credit cards, and now...

JOHN BREYAULT: They're no longer sort of a thank you for flying with a particular airline.

CHAPPELL: That's John Breyault with the International Consumers League (ph).

BREYAULT: The rewards ecosystem has allowed airlines to become, in many ways, banks that just happen to fly airplanes.

CHAPPELL: The idea is that when airlines create points, they're essentially creating a type of currency, and they control its value. Moshe Orenbuch is a research analyst at TD Cowen investment bank. He doesn't see airlines as banks.

MOSHE ORENBUCH: I think that might be a tad exaggerated.

CHAPPELL: But he agrees airlines use credit cards to focus on their most loyal customers, even when those customers aren't actually using an airline credit card to buy a plane ticket.

ORENBUCH: The vast majority of the spending is spending that's being done outside of that airline brand in order to accumulate points.

CHAPPELL: And Breyault says, in many cases, airlines don't have to provide anything in return for those points.

BREYAULT: A tremendous amount of airline rewards never actually get spent. It's what's called breakage, and that's basically free money.

CHAPPELL: Credit card companies pay airlines for each account, and Orenbuch says airlines also get paid when customers use perks.

ORENBUCH: For example, they get paid for the lounge access that the high-end cards get, and they get paid for the miles that the consumer earns.

CHAPPELL: With jet fuel costing far more than last year, credit card revenue is a bright spot for airlines. Last month, Delta said its American Express card program will bring in more than $9 billion this year. To put that in perspective, the airline predicts a pretax profit of 4.5 billion this year. Here's how Delta CEO Ed Bastian describes the relationship with Amex.

ED BASTIAN: They are our No. 1 partner in the world, and we are theirs.

CHAPPELL: And the programs keep evolving. Volodymyr Bilotkach is an associate professor of aviation management at Purdue University.

VOLODYMYR BILOTKACH: With American Airlines, if you buy the basic economy fare now, you don't get any points whatsoever.

CHAPPELL: Airlines get more revenue by unbundling services that used to be automatic, like checking a bag or choosing a seat. Then they treat those services as perks to reward status.

BILOTKACH: There is this kind of increasing differentiation between frequent and occasional fliers.

CHAPPELL: Consumer advocates say there are problems with the system. Airlines could simply devalue their points, for instance. Bilotkach says there are other risks.

BILOTKACH: As with any other credit card, you have to use your common sense.

CHAPPELL: He says you shouldn't pay high fees or overspend just to chase airline status. Bill Chappell, NPR News.

Why it is here: Reports on the new UK-EU treaties with a focus on the 10-year termination clause, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

New UK-EU treaties have 10-year termination clause, BBC understands

- Published

The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the treaties have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

- EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

- Published14 hours ago

- Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

- Published14 hours ago

- Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

- Published12 hours ago

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.

Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

item.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Examines the copyright dispute over the Stratocaster guitar, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster

Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments.

Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton.

The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads â Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments.

The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria.

The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954.

In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars.

Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.

Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music.

These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute.

When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers.

The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design.

But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in DÃ¼sseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection, external of the Stratocaster design in Germany.

The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The DÃ¼sseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections.

The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author".

It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms".

On its website, Fender announced in March, external the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced".

Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe.

One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products".

The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars.

The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians.

"Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments.

Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole.

"We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action."

The letter, he says, came as a shock.

"For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions."

In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier.

"As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action."

In June, Thomann the company started legal action against Fender, filing an "action of non-infringement" that said that Fender does not have a valid copyright claim to the Stat shape.

Thomann says that the DÃ¼sseldorf ruling was simply a default judgement based on missed deadlines and didn't represent a "comprehensive review of the legal claims".

For its part, Fender, which is majority-owned by Hawaii-based company Servco Pacific, says it has a responsibility to protect the Stratocaster's iconic design. In July, it sued Thomann in a German court, for copyright infringement.

In a statement to the BBC, Fender said it remained "confident" in the original DÃ¼sseldorf court judgement.

"Our preference has always been to keep lines of communication open and resolve these matters through constructive dialogue rather than litigation," it added.

With the legal cases continuing, Thomann says he believes it is important to get "legal clarity â not only for us but for the wider guitar industry."

"Ultimately, we want to help preserve an environment in which innovation, diversity and creative development can continue to thrive," he adds.

Thomann says he was taking legal action not just for his company, but for smaller music companies too.

"We used to be a small music shop ourselves," he says.

"Many of the smaller manufacturers, guitar makers and dealers affected simply don't have the financial and legal resources to conduct a legal dispute like this."

One such company is LSL Instruments, a family-owned boutique guitar maker in California. Its director of sales, Johny Miller, told me that when they first received Fender's letter they were "pretty terrified and blown away".…

Why it is here: Reports on the Los Angeles Lakers' deal with Kalshi, indicating the growing use of prediction markets in sports, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports. The team announced the news on Tuesday in a brief statement that hailed the partnership, but offered few details on what it will entail.

“We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen.

The announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets. The league officially embraced the platforms only a month ago, when it named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred exchanges. Kalshi has since moved quickly to turn that opening into team-level agreements, signing the Philadelphia 76ers in October before adding the Lakers this week.

The NBA’s overall positioning came as something of a surprise, given that it and the National Football League had largely held back while other major sports leagues signed agreements with prediction markets. Some of these platforms let users as young as 18 wager on event contracts, with sports making up the bulk of trading.

Other major sports organizations have mostly taken a welcoming approach. The National Hockey League became the first major North American professional sports league to strike prediction market deals in October 2025, signing multiyear agreements with Kalshi and Polymarket that included rights to league data, branding, and broadcast advertising. That push expanded to more teams last week, when seven NHL teams announced their own marketing deals with Novig. Others, including Major League Soccer, Major League Baseball, and UFC, have also struck deals with prediction markets.

The NFL, meanwhile, has remained as the odd one out.

In early October, the league filed a 24-page brief urging the Supreme Court to back state gambling regulators, who argue that sports prediction contracts should follow the same rules as traditional sports bets. At the heart of that dispute is whether the contracts are financial products governed by federal regulators or bets subject to state gambling laws. The league also raised concerns about cheating, insider trading, consumer protection, and risks to younger users.

The legal fight also hangs over the Lakers’ new partnership. California allows tribal casinos and a state lottery, but it has kept traditional sports betting off the table, with a bookmaking ban dating back more than a century. The state kept that prohibition in place after the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports betting in 2018, and voters rejected two legalization measures in 2022.

If the Supreme Court takes up the case and sides with state regulators, Kalshi could face new limits on offering sports contracts in California—complicating its push to reach fans in the Lakers’ home market.

Why it is here: Discusses the lower prices of cannabis during Thanksgiving, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis

This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.

But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.

Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.

In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.

Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.

As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.

A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.

On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.

Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.

"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."

The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.

In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.

It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.

"It's forced a race to the bottom," said Beau Whitney, the founder and chief economist at Whitney Economics. "What this is resulting in is great prices for the consumer, they're spending less and getting the same or more, so that's good for them on an affordability perspective. But it's hurting operators."

Though the industry has seen a slight rebound this year — an increase of about 5% in sales for the same period last year, Whitney's team found — forecasts for the end of 2026 and the outlook for 2027 remain relatively modest.

The biggest reason for this, Whitney said, is customer behavior.

Through the beginning of the 2020s, Whitney said, consumers would typically come into a dispensary with a set amount to spend. Their cannabis budget. If they got a discount, Whitney said, they'd add additional products into their carts to hit their budget.

But that began to change in 2024, as inflation rose and the cost of essentials, like gas, ballooned.

"Behavior changed literally overnight," Whitney said. "What they're doing is they're taking the discounts — and there's a lot of them now — and they're using that money to buy gas and buy groceries. So they're adjusting the amount that they purchase based on what's going on in their own personal economy."

The discount model, he said, has also forced prices down. With legal retailers competing for a pool of customers that has not seen rapid growth in years, discounts help draw people into stores. But they've also created a culture where customers expect them, several cannabis store owners said.

It's why doing well on a week like this one, as customers flood in for Green Wednesday deals, is essential for shop owners like The Forest's Christina Betancourt Johnson.

On Monday, the Baltimore store was stocked — with edibles and pre-rolls and other cannabis products, but also stacks of snacks for customers waiting in longer-than-usual lines, branded giveaways and samples of gummies to try (no weed in those).

A steady flow of customers wandered in. Some for their usual supplies, others for a little holiday shopping.

Employee Thomas Bourne loaded a vape into a paper bag for one of the dispensary's regular customers. That seemed a little light for the holiday, he observed, teasingly.

"Gotta come back for your cousin walk essentials, man," Bourne said. "'Tis the week."

The customer smiled, nodding. He'd be back.
